paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis (MMLA) is a mitochondrial neurodegenerative disorder. In the first patient with PNPLA8 mutations, reported by Saunders et al. (2015), it presented as progressive muscle weakness, hypotonia, seizures, poor weight gain, and lactic acidosis. Nakamura et al. (2024) reviewed current and previously reported patients and concluded that PNPLA8-related neurologic disease forms a continuum. At the severe end is developmental and/or degenerative epileptic-dyskinetic encephalopathy with congenital microcephaly and pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and at the milder end is childhood-onset neurodegeneration. A milder phenotype of adolescent-onset cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy has also been described (Burnyte et al., 2023).

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) reported a 23-year-old man with mitochondrial myopathy. He had a high-output circulatory state and cardiomyopathy that caused cardiac insufficiency 22 years before the skeletal myopathy appeared. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and accumulation of neutral lipids, which was confirmed histochemically and by thin-layer chromatography.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old girl with a suspected mitochondrial myopathy. She was asymptomatic in her first year and met all developmental milestones, although her parents noted toe-walking. A positive Gowers sign was noted at age 2 years, and by age 3 years she could no longer walk. Her fine motor skills declined, and her speech became dysarthric. She had proximal muscle weakness, tight heel cords, and dysmetria, and her hypotonicity progressed to spasticity. Later she developed complex partial seizures with recurrent left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. She had a persistently very lean body habitus and significant lactic acidosis requiring bicarbonate supplementation. The anion gap had been elevated (17 mmol/L) since age 5. At age 6, cerebrospinal fluid showed deficiency of 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. At age 7, blood lactic acid was 3.8 to 5.6 mmol/L (normal, 0.7-2.1) and pyruvic acid 0.18 to 0.32 mmol/L (normal, 0.08-0.16), with lactate:pyruvate ratios of 17.5 to 21.1. Brain MRI at 33 months showed subtle increased signal in the medial globus pallidus bilaterally, which was no longer seen 2 years later. A muscle biopsy at age 4 years showed variable fiber size with isolated small atrophic fibers and no ragged red fibers. On electron microscopy, mitochondria showed marked disarray of cristae and globular dense osmiophilic inclusions, and there were subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes. Secondary lysosomes containing residual bodies that appeared to be derived from mitochondria were increased.

paragraphs.text: Patient 2 of Shukla et al. (2018), born to nonconsanguineous parents of Indian/Fijian origin, developed normally until about 13 months of age. She then regressed, with episodes of epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures. She developed acquired microcephaly (head circumference 49 cm, -4.7 SD, at 15 years of age). She remained severely delayed and nonverbal, needed a gastrostomy tube, and developed choreiform movements, dystonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent muscle stretch reflexes, and severe contractures. Over a decade, MRI showed progressive volume loss in the cerebellum, brainstem, and bilateral parietal and occipital lobes, with thinning of the corpus callosum. MRS showed a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak. On electron microscopy, muscle showed enlarged, irregularly shaped mitochondria with surrounding membrane whorls. Blood lactate was elevated on several occasions, and at age 14 years growth and differentiation factor-15 was 1293 pg/ml (normal, less than 750). She also had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, severely reduced amplitudes with prolonged latencies on visual evoked potentials, and obstructive sleep apnea.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) reported 2 adult sibs with adolescence-onset ataxia, progressive sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and cognition that remained intact over time. The brother, now 49 years old, developed weakness and distal muscle atrophy of the lower limbs at age 14, together with ataxia and gait disturbance. He could not walk without assistance from age 17 and became nonambulant at age 44. Findings included tetraparesis, absent tendon reflexes in the lower limbs, bilateral Babinski signs, marked dysmetria, foot deformities, and sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy. At age 45 he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus, and his Mini-Mental State Examination score was 30/30. Brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy. His sister developed walking difficulty and lower limb weakness at age 14 years. At age 21 she had distal limb muscle atrophy, absent lower limb tendon reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, severe axial ataxia, appendicular dysmetria, and axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, and her cognition was normal.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals from 12 unrelated families. Frequent features included central hypotonia (13 of 13), dystonia (8 of 12), seizures (10 of 14), and cerebellar atrophy (12 of 12). The 8 patients from Families 1 to 8 formed a severe group. Their features included congenital microcephaly (5 of 7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7 of 7), peripheral spasticity (7 of 8), seizure onset within 7 months of age (8 of 8), a simplified gyral pattern (6 of 6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7 of 7), and severe progressive atrophy of the cerebral cortex (5 of 5). The 4 patients from Families 11 and 12 formed a mild group. All 4 learned to walk and later regressed, 3 had ataxia, and 3 had mild or no intellectual disability. They had little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Patients from Families 9 and 10 had intermediate severity. In skin fibroblasts from Patient 1, maximal mitochondrial respiration was significantly lower than in controls, but mitochondrial morphology was not altered.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) identified biallelic PNPLA8 variants in 14 individuals from 12 unrelated families using proband-only or trio exome or genome sequencing. One of these families had previously been reported by Denommé-Pichon et al. (2022). There were 14 different variants, 12 of them novel: 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic variants near an exon-intron boundary, and 2 missense. All had frequencies of less than 0.001% in population databases. In patient lymphoblastoid cells, the c.1625+3_1625+6del variant in Patient 1 caused skipping of exons 6 to 8, and the patient's fibroblasts showed a significant reduction in the 77-kD PNPLA8 isoform. Fibroblasts from Patient 6, who carried a frameshift variant (Glu296LysfsTer6), also showed a null effect. Cerebral organoids derived from Patient 1 induced pluripotent stem cells had fewer basal radial glial cells and fewer SATB2-positive upper-layer neurons than control organoids. Adding lysophosphatidic acid partly restored the number of basal radial glial cells. Two further individuals from a non-neurologic cohort, one with optic atrophy and one with nonsyndromic hearing loss, were homozygous for N-terminal frameshift variants that affect only the 88-kD isoform. The authors considered the significance of these variants undetermined.
